newsitem.title: USA: Deepwater prospects fuel bids in Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Deepwater prospects fuel bids in Gulf.

text.p: Independent oil and natural gas producers are expected to take the plunge into deeper waters on Wednesday as the federal government places blocks in the western Gulf of Mexico up for auction.

The annual lease sale is expected to attract modest interest in shallow blocks off the Texas and western Louisiana coasts, but aggressive bidding should emerge on several deepwater tracts, executives and analysts said.
The sale, to be held in New Orleans, is the first in which royalty relief is available on production in the western Gulf.

"I fully anticipate that out in deeper water, that there will be a lot of players. That's where the activity I think is going to be pretty hot and heavy," said John Williams, senior vice president of exploration and production at Louisiana Land and Exploration Co.

The lure of massive deepwater oil and natural gas fields has fuelled intense interest in recent lease sales by the U.S. Minerals Management Service, which regulates exploration and production in federal waters of the Gulf.
The most recent auction of central Gulf drilling sites in April drew a record $520.9 million bid on 924 tracts.

"This sale is not going to touch that, but it should do much better than last year's western sale," said Blake Wright, a Houston-based Offshore Data Services analyst who tracks Gulf leasing and drilling activity. "This is going to be a real good test for deepwater royalty relief."
Bids on deepwater Gulf tracts soared after the federal government exempted up to 87.5 million barrels of deepwater production from royalty payments to boost domestic production.
Drilling rights on 5,168 blocks covering more than 28.4 million acres on the outer continental shelf are up for sale in this latest round, with sealed bids to be opened Wednesday.

Deepwater tracts expected to generate the most intense bidding include the Garden Banks, East Breaks and Alaminos Canyon blocks in waters ranging from about 250 feet (75 meters) to 3,000 feet (915 meters) deep off the coast of Corpus Christi, Texas.
The major companies have charted a steady course into these deeper waters, but this year will be joined by some new players.

"I think you are going to see a whole bunch of new faces out there," LL&E's Williams said. "Back up on the shelf it's getting real tough and very competitive, and if we want to lower our risks and raise our sights on size of opportunity, we've just got to do this for our future."

While companies typically decline to discuss strategies for the sale, some expected to be active in the bidding include exploration arms of Shell Oil Co., Exxon Corp., Texaco Inc., Chevron Corp., Phillips Petroleum Co. and Amerada Hess Corp.
If recent lease sales are an accurate barometer, sources said the active independents could include Broken Hill Proprietary's domestic unit, Vastar Resources Inc. and newcomer Forest Oil Corp.
